KEY MESSAGE 1...A nor'easter passes offshore late Wednesday into 
Thursday, bringing a few showers to areas east of I-95. Otherwise, 
dry and breezy conditions prevail through the middle part of the 
week.

There were no notable changes to the near and short-term forecast 
during the overnight update. A broad 1030+ mb high pressure system 
situated northwest of southern New England will provide yet another 
dry day across the region. However, there will likely be more 
filtered sunshine today, especially across eastern portions of 
southern New England, while areas farther west are treated to 
another mainly clear day. 925 mb temperatures this afternoon are 
expected to range from +8C to +10C, and anticipate highs reaching 
well into the lower to middle 60s across interior areas, while the 
coastal plain remains in the upper 50s to lower 60s. In addition, 
winds increase due to a tightening pressure gradient between the 
aforementioned area of high pressure and a developing nor'easter off 
the North Carolina coast. There is good confidence that breezy to 
gusty northeast winds will be most prevalent east of I-95, with 
gusts of 20 to 30 mph. The strongest gusts, 30 to 40 mph, are 
expected along the east-facing Massachusetts coastline, Cape Cod, 
and the Islands. While previous guidance suggested a few gusts 
exceeding 45 mph across Nantucket, confidence in these stronger 
gusts has decreased as the latest guidance favors a farther offshore 
track.

These winds continue overnight and into Wednesday as the nor'easter 
strengthens and tracks northeast, while rain chances remain fairly 
low during this time frame. Clouds increase overnight into 
Wednesday, with the added cloud cover helping to moderate overnight 
lows. Temperatures across Cape Cod and the Islands remain in the 
upper 40s to lower 50s, while interior locations experience some 
clearing early in the night before clouds increase later. This 
should allow temperatures to fall into the upper 30s to lower 40s. 
Predominantly dry conditions continue into Wednesday, with 
temperatures slightly cooler than today, mainly due to increased 
cloud cover limiting diurnal heating. Wind conditions will be nearly 
identical to today. During this time frame, we can utilize high-
resolution guidance, including the CAMs, to get a better sense of 
how things may play out. There is a low chance for a few showers, 
mainly after 18z/2 PM Wednesday, across Nantucket, Martha's 
Vineyard, and outer Cape Cod, including Chatham.

Confidence remains high that a slow-moving nor'easter will track up 
the coast but remain far enough offshore to limit significant 
impacts to land. However, dangerous marine conditions are 
anticipated. As previous forecasters have mentioned, the NAM has 
shown the westernmost solution. The 20/00z run indicates that the 
NAM is coming more in line with the deterministic GFS, while the 
ECMWF remains somewhat farther east. Global ensembles also continue 
to indicate that this nor'easter will make its closest approach late 
Wednesday night into early Thursday morning before accelerating 
northeast into the northern Atlantic. Rain chances remain fairly low 
for most of southern New England, with the greatest chance for 
showers across the Cape and Islands from Wednesday afternoon into 
early Thursday morning. A few showers may also reach portions of 
eastern MA and RI, though most locations will remain dry. Even then, 
any rainfall is not expected to produce notable impacts. 
Nevertheless, while this will not be the quintessential nor'easter 
for those on land, it certainly will be for the marine community. 
Large waves of 7 to 13 feet are expected to build offshore, 
accompanied by gale-force winds out of the north-northeast to 
northeast. While astronomical tides are low, persistent wind and 
wave action may lead to beach erosion. Additional details on the 
hazardous marine conditions can be found in the marine discussion.

KEY MESSAGE 2...Fairly cool on Friday with a very low chance of an 
early morning shower. Otherwise, moderating temperatures and dry 
conditions are expected for the weekend into early next week.

As the nor'easter peels out to sea, strong high pressure settles in 
for the upcoming weekend. There is one interesting feature worth 
watching, although it is unlikely to cause more than a slight 
inconvenience. A mid-level cold pool associated with a robust 
northern-stream shortwave passes through early Friday. While PWATs 
will be limited by this time, a spot shower early Friday morning 
cannot be ruled out, with areas east of I-95 having the greatest 
chance. Otherwise, high pressure promotes sinking air and generally 
quiet weather this weekend into Monday of next week. With the cold 
pool aloft, Friday will be the coolest day, with highs in the lower 
50s. Depending on how quickly winds decouple, Saturday morning could 
feature a frosty start, with lows in the upper 20s to middle 30s.
